Coming from Stata

Source: vignettes/articles/coming-from-stata.Rmd
coming-from-stata.Rmd

中文版

For chapter navigation, search and expandable alternatives, open the Stata to R Reference. The book has English and Chinese editions with a language switch on each chapter. This page remains available as the single-page reference.

If you know Stata, you already know what you want to do; the question is how to say it in R. This page lists Stata commands next to the R code that does the same job, using tidystata where it has a Stata-style function and the standard package everywhere else.

Look it up from the console

findit() searches the same list from R. Type one Stata word bare, or quote anything longer. Stata’s abbreviations work.

findit(reg)
#> # Linear regression [stats]
#> Stata: regress y x1 x2
#> R:     fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = data)
#> # Note: summary(fit) shows the coefficient table; broom::tidy(fit) returns it as a data frame.
#> 
#> # 17 more examples. To see them all: findit(reg) |> print(n = Inf)
findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")
#> # Keep matched rows only [dplyr]
#> Stata: merge 1:1 id using data2, keep(match)
#> R:     inner_join(data1, data2, by = "id")
#> # Note: dplyr retains overlapping non-key columns with suffixes instead of Stata master values, creates no _merge, and does not enforce a declared 1:1 key constraint.
#> 
#> # merge() [base]: Merge two data frames (base R)
#>   Related Stata: merge
#> 
#> # 17 more examples. To see them all: findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)") |> print(n = Inf)

You can also look up an R function (findit(left_join)) or ask a question (findit("how do I remove duplicate rows")). The console shows the best matches; the returned table contains all matches. Call findit() for the whole list. Descriptions follow R’s language setting; English and Chinese queries both work.

Comma-separated names customize compatible examples, such as findit(tab, sex, region). The default shows one preferred answer when the task is clear; findit(tab) |> print(n = Inf) shows all variants, selected alternative R approaches, qualifications and source links. Package-qualified lookups such as findit(dplyr::filter) distinguish functions with the same name.

This reference contains 514 command families, 181 Stata functions and 3 operators, with 1716 distinct Stata examples and 1782 paired R examples. Abbreviations and alternative R implementations do not increase the command count. The R index describes 949 function/package pairs.

Use the command tables

The tables cover tidystata and other R packages, including modelling, reshaping, survey analysis and graphics. For panel lags and leads, tidystata provides stata_lag(), stata_lead() and stata_diff(); specify the time column and use .by to identify panels.

The index is alphabetical; tables are grouped by subject and sorted by command, preferred answer and example. A package named beside a snippet is needed to run that snippet, but findit() itself does not load or install reference packages. The label names the primary package, rather than every helper dependency; the R function index identifies additional functions and their packages.

A note that begins Differs from Stata means the R code does the same job, but a default, the missing-value handling, an estimator or the output layout differs; the note says how. Other notes are practical tips. Most R snippets are run against controlled checks when the catalogue is built; this tests the R code itself, not numerical agreement with Stata. Missing-value comparisons, weights, factor reference levels, join rules and standard-error corrections need particular care. Known gaps are explained explicitly, and related search results are not a translation of unsupported syntax.

In the tables below, data is your dataset, data1 and data2 are the master and using data of a merge, and fit is a fitted model. Most entries use dplyr, so attach it with library(dplyr) or library(tidyverse).

findit command
 
findit(command)
tidystata 		Find the R equivalent of a Stata command
Bare words and comma-separated names work: findit(tab, sex, region). Add hints such as findit(tab, gen), or quote full Stata syntax. One clear example is shown by default; print(n = Inf) reveals every match. findit() with no argument returns the whole list.

ksmirnov x, by(group)
 
ks.test(data$x[data$group == 0], data$x[data$group == 1])
stats 		Kolmogorov-Smirnov test of equal distributions
Differs from Stata: The R code assumes group codes 0 and 1; exact/asymptotic inference and tied-value handling can differ from Stata ksmirnov.
Stata reference · R reference 
ktau x y
 
cor.test(data$x, data$y, method = "kendall")
stats 		Kendall's tau
Differs from Stata: The rank coefficient has the same interpretation, but exact/asymptotic p-value selection and tie corrections may differ; match inference options separately.
Stata reference · R reference 
kwallis x, by(group)
 
kruskal.test(x ~ group, data = data)
stats 		Kruskal-Wallis test
Stata reference · R reference 
levelsof x
 
sort(unique(data$x))
base 		Distinct values of a variable
Differs from Stata: Store them for a loop: levels <- sort(unique(data$x)), then for (v in levels) { ... }. sort(unique()) excludes NA by default, but string ordering follows R collation and can differ from Stata sorting.
Stata reference · R reference 
list
 
print_all(data)
tidystata 		Print the first and last rows
Prints every row and column. Typing data prints the first rows; print_headtail(data) prints the first and last rows.
Stata reference · R reference 
list x
 
pull(data, x)
dplyr 		Print one variable
data$x does the same. select(data, x) keeps x as a one-column table.
Stata reference · R reference 
lookfor income
 
variables_search(data, "income")
tidystata 		Find variables by name or label
Stata reference · R reference 
mean x
 
summ(data, x, .stat = c("mean", "se"))
tidystata 		Mean with its standard error
Differs from Stata: t.test(data$x) also reports the confidence interval. The R snippet returns point summaries only (plus SE for mean); Stata also reports confidence intervals and estimation results.
Stata reference · R reference 
oneway y group
 
summary(aov(y ~ factor(group), data = data))
stats 		One-way analysis of variance
Differs from Stata: bartlett.test(y ~ group, data = data) gives the equal-variance test that oneway reports. aov() gives the ANOVA table but does not include the Bartlett equal-variance test printed by oneway; request bartlett.test() separately.
Stata reference · R reference 
pca x1 x2 x3
 
prcomp(na.omit(select(data, x1, x2, x3)), scale. = TRUE)
stats 		Principal components
Differs from Stata: Stata analyses the correlation matrix, so scale. = TRUE matches it. scale. = TRUE matches correlation PCA; signs of eigenvectors are arbitrary and the stored rotations and printed loadings have different normalization conventions.
Stata reference · R reference 
proportion x
 
prop.table(table(data$x))
base 		Proportion in each category
Differs from Stata: tab(data, x) shows the same percentages; prop.test() adds a confidence interval for one proportion. The R snippet returns point summaries only (plus SE for mean); Stata also reports confidence intervals and estimation results.
Stata reference · R reference 
prtest x == 0.5
 
prop.test(sum(data$x == 1, na.rm = TRUE), sum(!is.na(data$x)), p = 0.5, correct = FALSE)
stats 		Test of a proportion
Differs from Stata: correct = FALSE gives Stata's normal-approximation test without continuity correction. The uncorrected test statistic matches the normal approximation, but prop.test() confidence intervals use score inversion rather than the prtest Wald interval.
Stata reference · R reference 
pwcorr x1 x2 x3
 
pwcorr(data, x1, x2, x3)
tidystata 		Pairwise correlations
Differs from Stata: Gives r, n and p for each pair; .wide = TRUE gives the matrix. Base R: cor(select(data, x1, x2, x3), use = "pairwise.complete.obs"). pwcorr() returns pair counts and p-values in a tidy table; Stata prints a correlation matrix by default and needs options for additional reporting.
Stata reference · R reference 
ranksum x, by(group)
 
wilcox.test(x ~ group, data = data)
stats 		Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney) test
Differs from Stata: R can choose exact inference in small samples and applies continuity correction in its normal approximation; Stata defaults differ. Set exact and correct deliberately.
Stata reference · R reference 
signrank x = y
 
wilcox.test(data$x, data$y, paired = TRUE)
stats 		Wilcoxon signed-rank test
Differs from Stata: R can choose exact inference in small samples and applies continuity correction in its normal approximation; Stata defaults differ. Set exact and correct deliberately.

summ(data, x, .wt = w, .wt_type = "analytic")

summ(data, x, .detail = TRUE)

Stata reference · R reference 
capture command
 
capture(expression)
tidystata 		Run code and keep its result without stopping on an error
Differs from Stata: Returns the expression's result on success; on error, emits a failure message and returns invisible NULL. quiet = TRUE suppresses the notice, warnings and messages, but keeps printed output. Use capture(data <- update(data)) to preserve an existing object if the update fails; data <- capture(update(data)) assigns NULL on error. Separate assignments in a captured block keep the last completed update; a single assignment around a failed pipeline keeps the original target. Earlier effects are not rolled back. This adapts Stata capture, which suppresses all output.
